chapter_note.about: Sorting questions in GATE are mostly counting questions. You are given a small array and asked how many comparisons, swaps or passes a particular sort needs, or what the array looks like after a pass. Then come the cost facts: best and worst case, stable or not, and what quicksort does on bad pivots. This chapter takes the simple sorts first, then inversions, merge sort, quicksort partition and analysis, and finally the lower bound for comparison sorts and k-way merging.
chapter_note.simple: Think of sorting a pile of exam papers by roll number. You can pull out the smallest roll number again and again (selection), swap neighbours that are in the wrong order (bubble), or slide each new paper into its place in the sorted stack (insertion). Two smarter ways are splitting the pile and merging two sorted halves (merge sort), or splitting around one paper so that smaller ones go left and bigger ones go right (quicksort). Quicksort is fast unless the paper you pick as the splitter is always the smallest or the biggest one. And no method that only compares two papers at a time can ever beat about n log n comparisons.

cards.title: Selection, bubble, insertion mechanics
cards.simple: Imagine sorting a hand of playing cards in three different ways. In the first way you scan the whole hand, pull out the smallest card and put it at the front. In the second you walk along the row and swap any two neighbours that are the wrong way round, so the biggest card floats to the end. In the third you pick up the next card and slide it left into its place among the cards you have already sorted. All three are easy, but each one pays a different number of comparisons and swaps. In exam words: selection sort swaps the minimum to the front each pass, bubble sort swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs, and insertion sort shifts larger keys right to insert the next key.
cards.idea: A simple sort repeats one small move until the array is in order. **Selection** finds the smallest remaining key and swaps it to the front. **Bubble** swaps neighbours that are in the wrong order, so the largest key drifts to the end. **Insertion** takes the next key and slides it left into place among the keys already sorted.
cards.definition:
For an array of $n$ keys:

- **Selection sort:** pass $i$ scans the unsorted part and swaps the minimum to position $i$. Comparisons are always $\binom n2=\frac{n(n-1)}2$. Swaps are at most $n-1$.
- **Bubble sort:** pass $p$ compares $n-p$ neighbouring pairs. Every swap removes exactly one inversion. With early exit it stops after a pass with no swap.
- **Insertion sort:** each key is compared with the sorted keys on its left and moves past every bigger one. Each shift is one comparison, plus one failing comparison when the key stops before the front.
cards.intuition_full: Think of what each sort has already guaranteed after $k$ passes. Selection has the $k$ smallest keys in their final places at the front. Bubble has the $k$ largest keys in their final places at the back. Insertion has the first $k+1$ keys sorted among themselves, but they may still move later. That one sentence explains most counting questions. Selection never looks at the order of the data, so it always does the same comparisons. Bubble and insertion react to the data, so a nearly sorted array makes them fast. A second picture: selection is a talent contest where the winner is picked each round, bubble is a queue where neighbours keep swapping places, and insertion is filing papers into a folder one at a time.

examples.setup: Run **one pass** of each simple sort on `[8, 3, 6, 2, 5]`. Which key is final after the pass, and how many comparisons and swaps (or shifts) did it cost?
steps: Three copies of `[8, 3, 6, 2, 5]`. Each sort will do its own first pass.
**Selection:** scan all five keys (4 comparisons) and find the smallest, 2 at index 3. Swap it with index 0: `[2, 3, 6, 8, 5]`. One swap, and 2 is final.
**Bubble:** compare neighbours left to right. 8>3, 8>6, 8>2, 8>5 all swap, so 8 travels to the end: `[3, 6, 2, 5, 8]`. That is 4 comparisons and 4 swaps, and 8 is final.
**Insertion:** take the key 3 (index 1). The left key 8 is bigger, so shift 8 right and drop 3 into the gap: `[3, 8, 6, 2, 5]`. One comparison and one shift. Only the first two keys are sorted.
Selection fixes the **front**, bubble fixes the **back**, insertion fixes nothing yet but keeps a sorted prefix. The costs differ: 4 and 1 swap, 4 and 4, 1 and 1 shift.
examples.answer: After one pass: selection `[2, 3, 6, 8, 5]` (4 comparisons, 1 swap), bubble `[3, 6, 2, 5, 8]` (4 comparisons, 4 swaps), insertion `[3, 8, 6, 2, 5]` (1 comparison, 1 shift).

examples.setup: Bubble sort with early exit (stop after a pass that makes no swap) runs on `[2, 6, 3, 1, 5, 4]`. How many comparisons and how many swaps does it make in total?
steps: Pass 1 compares 5 pairs. The 6 moves right past 3, 1, 5 and 4 (4 swaps): `[2, 3, 1, 5, 4, 6]`.
Pass 2 compares 4 pairs, since the last cell is final. 3 swaps with 1, and 5 swaps with 4 (2 swaps): `[2, 1, 3, 4, 5, 6]`.
Pass 3 compares 3 pairs. 2 swaps with 1 (1 swap): `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`. The array is sorted now, but the algorithm cannot know that yet.
Pass 4 compares 2 pairs and finds nothing to swap, so it stops. This **verification pass** is the one people forget.
Comparisons: 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 14. Swaps: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7, which equals the number of inversions in the input.
examples.answer: 14 comparisons and 7 swaps. Stopping at the sorted pass (pass 3) would wrongly give 12 comparisons.

examples.setup: Insertion sort runs on `[4, 6, 7, 1]`. A student claims comparisons = shifts + (n - 1). Count the comparisons properly.
steps: Key 6: compare with 4. 4 is not bigger, so the inner loop stops. 1 comparison, 0 shifts.
Key 7: compare with 6. Not bigger, so it stops. 1 comparison, 0 shifts.
Key 1: compare with 7, 6 and 4. All three are bigger, so each shifts right. After the third shift the position is the front of the array and there is nothing left to compare. 3 comparisons, 3 shifts.
Total comparisons: 1 + 1 + 3 = 5. Total shifts: 3. The student formula gives 3 + 3 = 6, which is wrong.
examples.answer: 5 comparisons and 3 shifts. The "extra failing comparison" exists only for keys that stop before reaching the front. Key 1 reaches the front, so it has none.

cards.title: Complexity, stability, in-place
cards.simple: Picture three people tidying a bookshelf that is already tidy. The first still checks every pair of books, because that is how their routine works. The second walks along the shelf once, sees nothing out of place and stops. So a sort's cost depends on the routine and on how messy the input is. Two more questions matter. Does the sort keep identical books in their starting order? That is called stable. Does it need a second shelf to work on? If not, it is in place. In exam words: selection sort is $\Theta(n^2)$ always, insertion sort is $\Theta(n)$ best and $\Theta(n^2)$ worst, merge sort is $\Theta(n\log n)$ always. Insertion, bubble and merge are stable; selection, quick and heap are not.
cards.idea: The **running time** of a sort is counted in comparisons. The **best case** is the cheapest input, the **worst case** the most expensive. A sort is **stable** if equal keys keep their input order, and **in place** if it uses $O(1)$ extra memory. Insertion sort is fast on nearly sorted input, selection sort never speeds up, and merge sort always costs about $n\log n$.
cards.definition:
| Sort | Best | Worst | Stable | Extra space |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Selection | $\Theta(n^2)$ | $\Theta(n^2)$ | no | $O(1)$ |
| Bubble | $\Theta(n)$ with flag | $\Theta(n^2)$ | yes | $O(1)$ |
| Insertion | $\Theta(n)$ | $\Theta(n^2)$ | yes | $O(1)$ |
| Merge | $\Theta(n\log n)$ | $\Theta(n\log n)$ | yes | $O(n)$ |
| Quick | $\Theta(n\log n)$ | $\Theta(n^2)$ | no | $O(\log n)$ stack |
| Heap | $\Theta(n\log n)$ | $\Theta(n\log n)$ | no | $O(1)$ |

$n$ is the number of keys. An algorithm is **adaptive** if it runs faster on input that is closer to sorted.
cards.intuition_full: Every comparison sort has to find the final order. Selection sort does it by brute force: it searches for the minimum from scratch every pass, so it learns nothing from nearly sorted input. Insertion sort reuses what it knows. If the next key is not smaller than its left neighbour, nothing further left can be bigger, so it stops. That is why its cost is $n$ plus the number of inversions. Merge sort has $\log_2 n$ levels and every level touches all $n$ keys once, so it costs $n\log n$ whatever the order. Quicksort has the same shape, but bad pivots make the tree lopsided and push the number of levels towards $n$. Stability breaks when an algorithm swaps keys that are far apart, because the jump can leap an equal key. Selection, quicksort partitioning and heap sort all do such jumps.

examples.setup: The three simple sorts run on 6 keys. Count their comparisons on the reversed input `[6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1]` and on the sorted input `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`. Bubble sort stops after a pass with no swap.
steps: Reversed input: every pair is out of order. Selection makes 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15 comparisons, bubble makes 15, and insertion makes 15 because each key travels to the front.
Now the sorted input `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`. Selection does not look at the order of the data, so it still makes 15 comparisons.
Bubble with early exit: pass 1 compares 5 pairs, swaps nothing, and stops. That is 5 comparisons.
Insertion: each of the 5 later keys is compared once with its left neighbour and stays put. That is 5 comparisons.
Best case is $n-1=5$ for insertion and for bubble with early exit. The worst case is $\binom n2 = 15$ for all three. Selection has no best case.
examples.answer: Reversed: 15, 15, 15. Sorted: selection 15, bubble 5, insertion 5.

examples.setup: The records `[2a, 2b, 1]` have two equal keys, tagged a and b in input order. Run selection sort and insertion sort. Which one keeps 2a before 2b, so that it is **stable**?
steps: Selection pass 1 finds the minimum 1 at index 2 and swaps it with index 0. The array becomes `[1, 2b, 2a]`, and the two 2s have crossed over.
Pass 2 compares 2b with 2a. Neither is smaller, so nothing moves. Final: `[1, 2b, 2a]`. The order of equal keys changed, so selection sort is **not stable**.
Insertion sort on the same input: key 2b meets 2a. 2a is not strictly bigger, so 2b stays. Then key 1 shifts 2b and 2a right by one place each: `[1, 2a, 2b]`.

Insertion sort only moves a key past **strictly bigger** keys, so equal keys never cross. It is stable. Bubble sort (swap only if strictly greater) and merge sort (take the left key on a tie) are stable as well. Quicksort and heap sort are not.
examples.answer: Insertion sort is stable (`[1, 2a, 2b]`). Selection sort is not (`[1, 2b, 2a]`).

examples.setup: Bubble sort is written with two nested loops and **no** swapped flag. The input is already sorted and $n=8$. How many comparisons does it make, and is its best case $O(n)$?
steps: Without the flag the loops never learn that the array is sorted. Pass $p$ compares $n-p$ pairs whatever the data.
Total: 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 28 comparisons and 0 swaps.
With the early-exit flag, pass 1 finds no swap and stops after 7 comparisons.
So the $O(n)$ best case belongs to bubble sort **with** the flag. Without it, the best case is still $\Theta(n^2)$.
examples.answer: 28 comparisons. The best case is $\Theta(n^2)$ without the flag, and 7 comparisons with it.

how: Name the sort and the input shape (sorted, reversed, all equal, random).
Selection: $\binom n2$ comparisons whatever the input. Insertion: $n-1$ on sorted input, $\binom n2$ on reversed.
Merge sort: $n\log_2 n$ worst, $\frac n2\log_2 n$ on sorted input. Quicksort with the first or last pivot on sorted input is the worst case.
For stability, remember the unstable three: selection, quick, heap. Insertion, bubble and merge are stable.
cards.mistake: Assuming sorted input is fast for every sort, or calling selection sort or quicksort stable. Selection sort does the same work on sorted input, and quicksort with the first or last element as pivot hits its worst case there. Only insertion sort (and bubble with a flag) speed up.
edge_cases: Bubble sort without the swapped flag is $\Theta(n^2)$ even on sorted input.
Merge sort is stable only if a tie takes the left element (`<=`). With `<` it becomes unstable.
Average case of quicksort is $\Theta(n\log n)$, the worst case is $\Theta(n^2)$. Both statements are true.
Merge sort is not in place ($O(n)$ extra), and quicksort uses an $O(\log n)$ stack on average, so 'in place' has a strict and a loose meaning.
connections: **Inversions** (next card) gives the exact formula: insertion sort time is $n$ plus the inversions.
**Algo complexity** (algo.complexity) is where the $\Theta$, $O$ and $\Omega$ notation comes from.
Quicksort's worst case is analysed in the card **Quicksort analysis**.

check.q: A sort makes 10 comparisons on a sorted array of 11 keys and 55 on the reversed one. Which sort could it be?
check.a: Insertion sort (or bubble sort with the flag): $n-1=10$ and $\binom{11}2=55$. Selection sort would make 55 on both.

check.q: Insertion sort runs on a sorted array of 1024 keys. How many comparisons does it make?
Which of merge sort, quicksort and insertion sort has $\Theta(n\log n)$ worst case, and which of them is unstable?
check.a: Only merge sort has the $n\log n$ worst case. Quicksort is the unstable one.

cards.title: Inversions
cards.simple: Line up a class by roll number, but a few students stand in the wrong order. Call a pair of students 'out of order' when the one in front should come later. If two neighbours swap places, exactly one out-of-order pair gets fixed, no more and no less. So the number of out-of-order pairs tells you how many neighbour swaps it takes to sort the line. That is the whole idea. In exam words: an inversion is a pair $i<j$ with $a[i]>a[j]$, and both the swaps of bubble sort and the shifts of insertion sort equal the number of inversions.
cards.idea: An **inversion** is a pair of keys in the wrong order: the bigger one stands to the left. Sorted input has 0 inversions and reversed input has the most, $\binom n2$. Bubble sort makes one swap per inversion, and insertion sort makes one shift per inversion.
cards.definition:
For an array $a[1..n]$ of distinct keys:

$$\text{inv}(a)=\#\{(i,j): i<j,\ a[i]>a[j]\}$$

- $0\le \text{inv}(a)\le \binom n2$.
- Bubble swaps $=\text{inv}(a)$. Insertion shifts $=\text{inv}(a)$. Insertion time is $\Theta(n+\text{inv}(a))$.
- A random permutation has $\binom n2/2$ inversions on average.
- With equal keys, only strictly bigger pairs count.
cards.intuition_full: Why does one adjacent swap remove exactly one inversion? Swapping neighbours $x$ and $y$ (with $x>y$) changes only the order of that pair. Every other key stays on the same side of both $x$ and $y$, so no other pair changes. The count drops by exactly 1, so you need exactly inv swaps to reach 0. Insertion sort is the same story in slow motion: when key $k$ slides left past $m$ bigger keys, it removes exactly the $m$ inversions that $k$ owned. Counting inversions per key (bigger keys on the left) is therefore the quickest way to get the total shifts. The average of $\binom n2/2$ comes from symmetry: each pair is out of order in half of all permutations.

examples.setup: An **inversion** is a pair of positions $i<j$ with $a[i]>a[j]$. Count the inversions of `[3, 5, 1, 4, 2]`, and predict how many swaps bubble sort and how many shifts insertion sort make.
steps: For every key, count the bigger keys that stand to its **left**. Each one is an inversion.
Key 3 has nothing bigger on its left, and key 5 has none either. Count so far: 0.
Key 1: the bigger keys on its left are 3 and 5. That adds 2. Total 2.
Key 4: only 5 is bigger on its left. That adds 1. Total 3.
Key 2: the keys 3, 5 and 4 on its left are bigger. That adds 3. Total 6.
The inversions are (3,1), (3,2), (5,1), (5,4), (5,2), (4,2): 6 pairs. Each bubble swap fixes one pair, and each insertion shift fixes one pair, so both do 6.

cards.title: Merge sort and the merge step
cards.simple: Two checkout queues are each sorted by shoe size. To make one sorted queue, look only at the two people at the front. The smaller shoe size steps into the new queue. Repeat. Each step costs exactly one comparison. When one queue empties, the other one walks straight in with no more comparisons. Merge sort applies this again and again: split the list in half, sort each half the same way, then merge. In exam words: merging sorted lists of sizes $m$ and $n$ takes at most $m+n-1$ comparisons, and merge sort satisfies $T(n)=2T(n/2)+\Theta(n)$.
cards.idea: **Merging** two sorted lists takes one comparison per output key, until one list runs out. **Merge sort** splits the array in half, sorts both halves recursively, then merges them. It always takes $\Theta(n\log n)$ time and uses $O(n)$ extra space. It is stable.
cards.definition:
- **Merge of sizes $m$ and $n$:** at most $m+n-1$ comparisons and at least $\min(m,n)$. The leftover tail is copied for free.
- **Merge sort recurrence:** $T(n)=2T(n/2)+(n-1)$ comparisons in the worst case, giving $n\log_2 n - n + 1$ when $n$ is a power of 2.
- **Best case** (sorted input): each merge uses only $s$ comparisons for halves of size $s$, so $\frac n2\log_2 n$ in total.
- **Stable** if a tie takes the left key first (`<=`).
cards.intuition_full: Why $m+n-1$? Every comparison puts exactly one key into the output, and the last key never needs a comparison, because by then the other list is empty. So the output has $m+n$ keys but at most $m+n-1$ of them were decided by comparing. Why does the whole sort cost $n\log n$? Halving $n$ gives $\log_2 n$ levels. At each level the merges together touch all $n$ keys, so each level costs about $n$ comparisons. A tournament picture helps: the two fronts are two players, the winner enters the final ranking, and the loser stays for the next match. For the exact worst-case count, each level contributes $n$ minus the number of merges at that level. The sum is $n\log_2 n-(1+2+4+\dots+n/2)=n\log_2 n-n+1$.

examples.setup: Merge the sorted lists `L = [3, 7, 8]` and `R = [1, 5, 9, 12]` into one sorted list. Count the comparisons.
steps: Keep one finger on the front of each list. Each round, compare the two fronts and move the smaller key to the output. Fingers start at 3 and 1.
Compare 3 and 1: output **1**. The R finger moves to 5. Comparisons: 1.
Compare 3 and 5: output **3**. The L finger moves to 7. Comparisons: 2.
Compare 7 and 5: output **5**. The R finger moves to 9. Comparisons: 3.
Compare 7 and 9: output **7**. The L finger moves to 8. Comparisons: 4.
Compare 8 and 9: output **8**. Now L is empty. Comparisons: 5.
Copy the rest of R (9 and 12) with no more comparisons. Output `[1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 12]`.
examples.answer: 5 comparisons. The most any merge of 3 and 4 keys can need is $3+4-1=6$.

Merge `[3,8]` and `[6,7]`: 3<6, 8>6, 8>7, then the right run is empty. 3 comparisons, giving `[3,6,7,8]`.

steps: The last merge always joins everything: $24-1=23$ comparisons, whatever the order. Only the first merge changes.
Merge 12 and 7 first: 18 comparisons, then 19 with 5: 23. Total 41.
Merge 12 and 5 first: 16 comparisons, then 17 with 7: 23. Total 39.
Merge 7 and 5 first: 11 comparisons, then 12 with 12: 23. Total 34.
Merging the two **smallest** lists first is cheapest. This is the same greedy idea as Huffman coding.
examples.answer: Merge 7 and 5 first. The total is 34 comparisons, against 39 and 41 for the other orders.

cards.title: Quicksort partition
cards.simple: Imagine a teacher splitting a class around one student, the pivot, who is 150 cm tall. Everyone shorter goes to the left of the pivot and everyone taller goes to the right. Inside each side the order is still random, but the pivot student now stands exactly where they will end up in the sorted line. Quicksort repeats this on the left group and on the right group. The partition step does all the real work. In exam words: partition rearranges the array around a pivot in $\Theta(n)$, so that smaller keys are on the left, bigger keys on the right, and (for Lomuto) the pivot is in its final sorted position.
cards.idea: **Partition** picks a pivot and rearranges the array so that keys <= pivot come first, then the pivot, then keys > pivot. In **Lomuto** partition the pivot is the last key, one pointer scans and another marks the boundary of the small keys. In **Hoare** partition two pointers walk in from both ends and swap misplaced pairs.
cards.definition:
**Lomuto** (pivot $=a[hi]$): keep $b$ = number of keys $\le$ pivot seen so far. For $j=lo..hi-1$: if $a[j]\le$ pivot, swap $a[b]$ and $a[j]$ and do $b$++. Finally swap $a[b]$ with the pivot. The pivot ends at index $b$, and a partition of $m$ keys makes $m-1$ comparisons.

**Hoare** (pivot $=a[lo]$): $i$ moves right while $a[i]<$ pivot, $j$ moves left while $a[j]>$ pivot. Swap while $i<j$. It returns a split index, but the pivot itself need not sit at the split.

Both take $\Theta(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra space. Neither is stable.
cards.intuition_full: Lomuto's invariant is easy to say: at any time the array has three zones. Indices below $b$ hold keys $\le$ pivot, indices from $b$ up to $j-1$ hold keys $>$ pivot, and indices from $j$ on are unseen. When the scan finds a small key, swapping it with $a[b]$ exchanges it with the first big key, which moves that big key to the end of the big zone. That keeps the invariant. At the end the pivot is swapped into $a[b]$, and it lands between the two zones. So its index is the count of keys smaller than or equal to it. Hoare's partition is the same idea with two scanners: the left scanner finds a key that belongs on the right, the right scanner finds one that belongs on the left, and they trade. Hoare does fewer swaps in practice, but it does not leave the pivot at the split.

examples.setup: Run Lomuto partition (pivot = last key) on `[5, 9, 2, 7, 1, 6, 4]`. Scan `j` from the left. `b` is the slot where the next small key goes. Find the final array and the pivot index.
steps: The pivot is the last key, 4. Set `b = 0` (no small keys yet) and start the scan at `j = 0`.
`j = 0`: 5 > 4, skip. `j = 1`: 9 > 4, skip. Nothing moves and `b` stays 0.
`j = 5`: 6 > 4, skip. The scan is over after 6 comparisons.
Swap the pivot with `a[b]`, that is `a[2]` and `a[6]`: `[2, 1, 4, 7, 9, 6, 5]`.
Everything left of index 2 is <= 4 and everything right is > 4. The pivot sits at its **final** sorted position, index 2.
examples.answer: `[2, 1, 4, 7, 9, 6, 5]`, pivot at index 2, after 6 comparisons.

examples.setup: Hoare partition with the **first** key as pivot runs on `[5, 3, 8, 6, 2, 7, 1, 4]`. Pointer `i` moves right until `a[i] >= 5`, pointer `j` moves left until `a[j] <= 5`, and they swap while `i < j`. What is the array after the partition, and is the pivot in its final place?
steps: Pivot = 5. `i` stops at index 0 (5 >= 5) and `j` stops at index 7 (4 <= 5). Swap: `[4, 3, 8, 6, 2, 7, 1, 5]`.
`i` skips 3 and stops at index 2 (8 >= 5). `j` moves left and stops at index 6 (1 <= 5). Swap: `[4, 3, 1, 6, 2, 7, 8, 5]`.
`i` stops at index 3 (6 >= 5). `j` skips 7 and stops at index 4 (2 <= 5). Swap: `[4, 3, 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 5]`.
`j` moves to index 3 (2 <= 5) and `i` moves to index 4 (6 >= 5). Now `i >= j`, so the partition ends with split index `j = 3`.
The left part `[4, 3, 1, 2]` has keys <= 5 and the right part `[6, 7, 8, 5]` has keys >= 5. The pivot 5 is **not** at index 3, so Hoare does not place the pivot.
examples.answer: `[4, 3, 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 5]`, split after index 3. The pivot is not in its final position.

examples.setup: Lomuto partition (last key as pivot) runs on the already sorted array `[2, 3, 5, 8, 9]`. What happens, and what does it mean for quicksort?
steps: The pivot is 9, the largest key. Every key from index 0 to 3 is <= 9.
Each of the four scans swaps `a[b]` with itself (b = j), so nothing really moves and `b` ends at 4.
The final pivot swap swaps index 4 with itself. The array is unchanged and the pivot index is 4.
The split is 4 keys on the left and 0 on the right. Repeating this on 4 keys, then 3, then 2 gives $4+3+2+1$ comparisons, which is quadratic.
examples.answer: The array stays `[2, 3, 5, 8, 9]` with pivot index 4: a 4 : 0 split. Sorted input is the worst case for a last-key pivot.

cards.title: Quicksort analysis
cards.simple: Imagine cutting a long rope into pieces, one cut at a time. If every cut lands in the middle, you need only a few rounds of cutting. If every cut chops off a tiny scrap, you need as many rounds as there are pieces. Quicksort is like that. The pivot is the cut, and its quality decides the speed. A random pivot is usually good enough, so the typical case is fast and only unlucky or ordered input is slow. In exam words: quicksort is $\Theta(n\log n)$ for balanced or random pivots and $\Theta(n^2)$ when the split is always $0:n-1$, for example sorted input with a first or last pivot.
cards.idea: Quicksort's cost is set by the **split sizes**. A split of $0:n-1$ every time gives $T(n)=T(n-1)+n$, which is $\Theta(n^2)$. A split at a fixed ratio, even $1:9$, gives $\Theta(n\log n)$. With a random pivot the expected cost is also $\Theta(n\log n)$, about $1.39\,n\log_2 n$ comparisons.
cards.definition:
- **Worst case:** $T(n)=T(n-1)+(n-1)$, so $\binom n2$ comparisons. It happens when the pivot is always the minimum or maximum, e.g. sorted input with first or last pivot.
- **Best case:** $T(n)=2T(n/2)+(n-1)$, about $n\log_2 n$.
- **Any fixed ratio** $T(n)=T(\alpha n)+T((1-\alpha)n)+n$ is $\Theta(n\log n)$.
- **Random pivot:** the probability of a worst possible split is $2/n$. The expected comparisons are about $2n\ln n\approx1.39\,n\log_2 n$.
- **Stack:** $O(n)$ worst case, $O(\log n)$ if you recurse on the smaller part first.
cards.intuition_full: Draw the recursion tree. Each level of the tree partitions keys that together add up to at most $n$, so one level costs at most about $n$. The total cost is therefore $n$ times the depth. A balanced tree has depth $\log_2 n$. A lopsided tree has depth up to $n$. If the split is always $1:9$, the deepest path shrinks by a factor of $9/10$ each time, so its depth is $\log_{10/9} n$, which is still $\Theta(\log n)$. This is why only a split of $0:n-1$ (or close to it, like a fixed number of keys) is truly bad. For the random pivot, a second picture: two keys are compared at most once, and only when one of them is picked as pivot before anything between them. Keys far apart in rank rarely meet. Adding these probabilities gives $2n\ln n$.

examples.setup: Quicksort partitions 7 keys with a partition that costs (size - 1) comparisons. Compare the total on a **sorted** array with first-key pivot (split 0 : size-1 every time) against a perfect median pivot.
steps: Sorted array, first-key pivot, 7 keys: the pivot is the smallest key, so the split is 0 and 6. The partition costs 6 comparisons. Running total: 6.
The 6 remaining keys split 0 and 5, then 5 split 0 and 4. Those partitions cost 5 and 4. Running total: 6 + 5 + 4 = 15.
The chain goes on through 4, 3, 2 keys: 3 + 2 + 1 more. Total: 21 = $\binom 72$, with a recursion tree that is 7 levels deep.
Now a perfect median pivot on 7 keys. The split is 3 and 3, and the partition costs 6 comparisons. Running total: 6.
Each 3-key part splits 1 and 1 with 2 comparisons, so 2 + 2 = 4 more. Single keys cost nothing. Total: 6 + 4 = 10, with a tree that is only 3 levels deep.
Bad splits give $T(n)=T(n-1)+n-1=\Theta(n^2)$. Balanced splits give $T(n)=2T(n/2)+n-1=\Theta(n\log n)$. The recursion tree decides the cost.
examples.answer: Sorted input: 21 comparisons (quadratic). Median pivot: 10 comparisons ($n\log n$ shape).

examples.setup: A quicksort variant always splits a part of size $m$ into $m/5$ and $4m/5$ keys, with a partition cost of $m$. Give the recurrence and the running time. How deep is the recursion tree for $n=1000$?
steps: Recurrence: $T(n)=T(n/5)+T(4n/5)+n$.
In the recursion tree, the sizes on one level add up to at most $n$, so every level costs at most $n$.
The deepest path always follows the 4/5 branch. It ends when $(4/5)^k\cdot 1000\le 1$, which gives $k\ge \ln 1000/\ln 1.25 \approx 30.96$, so 31 levels.
The shortest path follows the 1/5 branch and has depth $\log_5 1000\approx 4.3$. So at least 4 levels are full, each costing $n$.
Total cost is between $4n$ and $31n$ for $n=1000$. In general it is $\Theta(n\log n)$, because any fixed ratio gives logarithmic depth.
examples.answer: $\Theta(n\log n)$. For $n=1000$ the tree is 31 levels deep along its longest path.

examples.setup: Quicksort runs on a sorted array of $n=1000$ keys with a last-key pivot, using plain recursion on both parts. How deep does the call stack get? How can it be kept small?
steps: Each partition leaves 999, then 998, then 997 keys on one side and nothing on the other. The calls nest 999 deep.
The time is $\Theta(n^2)$, and the stack is $\Theta(n)$ as well. A large $n$ could overflow it.
Fix: recurse on the **smaller** part first and loop on the bigger one (a tail call). The smaller part has at most half of the keys.
After each nested call the size at least halves: 1000, 500, 250, 125, 62, 31, 15, 7, 3, 1. That is at most $\lfloor\log_2 1000\rfloor = 9$ nested calls.
examples.answer: 999 nested calls with plain recursion. At most 9 with smaller-part-first. The running time is still quadratic on this input.

cards.title: Lower bound and k-way merge
cards.simple: Think of the game 'guess my number' with yes/no questions. If I choose one of 8 numbers, you need at least 3 questions, because each question can at most halve the options. Sorting is the same game. Your unknown is the correct order of the keys, and each comparison is a yes/no question. With $n$ keys there are $n!$ possible orders, so you need about $\log_2 n!$ questions. A second trick: if several lists are already sorted, a small heap of their front keys picks the next smallest cheaply. In exam words: any comparison sort needs $\Omega(n\log n)$ comparisons, and merging $k$ sorted lists with a heap takes $O(n\log k)$.
cards.idea: A **comparison sort** can be drawn as a binary **decision tree** with at least $n!$ leaves, one per final order. A tree with $n!$ leaves has height at least $\log_2 n!$, which is $\Theta(n\log n)$. So no comparison sort beats $n\log n$ in the worst case. To merge $k$ sorted lists, keep a min-heap of the $k$ current heads: each output costs $O(\log k)$.
cards.definition:
- **Lower bound:** worst-case comparisons $\ge\lceil\log_2 n!\rceil=\Omega(n\log n)$. Stirling: $\log_2 n!=n\log_2 n-1.44n+O(\log n)$.
- **k-way merge:** $n$ keys in $k$ sorted lists, one min-heap of size $k$: $O(n\log k)$ time and $O(k)$ extra heap space.
- The bound applies only to sorts that learn the order from comparisons. Counting sort and radix sort do not compare keys, so they can be linear.
cards.intuition_full: Why $n!$ leaves? Two different input orders must end in different leaves, since the algorithm must rearrange them differently. A tree of height $h$ has at most $2^h$ leaves, because each comparison has two outcomes. So $2^h\ge n!$. Taking the logarithm gives $h\ge\log_2 n!$. To see that this is about $n\log_2 n$, note that $n!\ge(n/2)^{n/2}$, because half of the factors are at least $n/2$. Then $\log_2 n!\ge\frac n2\log_2\frac n2$. For the k-way merge, the heap is the same tournament-tree idea: the winner of $k$ list fronts is found in $\log_2 k$ steps instead of $k$ steps, and the next key of that list takes its place. A plain scan of the $k$ heads would cost $O(nk)$.

examples.setup: Draw the decision tree of a comparison sort for three keys $a$, $b$, $c$. How many leaves must it have, and what is the least possible height?
steps: A comparison sort asks yes/no questions. The root asks "is $a<b$?". The left branch means yes and the right branch no.
Second level: if $a<b$ ask $b$ against $c$. If $a>b$ ask $a$ against $c$. Two leaves, `abc` and `bac`, can already be decided.
Third level: the remaining nodes ask one more question each and produce the leaves `acb`, `cab`, `bca` and `cba`.
Each leaf is one final order of the three keys. There are $3!=6$ possible orders, so the tree needs at least 6 leaves.
The longest root-to-leaf path has 3 comparisons. That is the worst case for this sort.
A binary tree of height $h$ has at most $2^h$ leaves. So $2^h\ge 6$ forces $h\ge\lceil\log_2 6\rceil=3$. No comparison sort for 3 keys can do better than 3 comparisons.
examples.answer: 6 leaves, height at least 3. So 3 comparisons are needed in the worst case.

examples.setup: $n=128$ keys are spread over $k=8$ sorted lists. They are merged into one list by repeatedly taking the smallest of the 8 current list heads with a min-heap of size 8. Estimate the work, and compare with sorting all 128 keys from scratch.
steps: The heap holds one key from each list: its current head. Its size is $k=8$.
Each output step removes the smallest head and inserts the next key of the same list. Each heap operation costs $O(\log k)$, and $\log_2 8=3$ levels.
There are $n=128$ output steps, so the work is $n\log_2 k=128\cdot3=384$ level steps.
Sorting 128 keys from scratch costs $n\log_2 n=128\cdot7=896$ level steps. The merge is cheaper because the lists are already sorted.
In general the merge costs $\Theta(n\log k)$. If $k=\log n$ lists are merged, this is $n\log\log n$.
examples.answer: $\Theta(n\log k)=384$ level steps, against 896 for a full sort.

examples.setup: A student says the least number of comparisons needed to sort 5 keys is $\lceil 5\log_2 5\rceil=12$. Find the true information bound.
steps: The bound is $\lceil\log_2 n!\rceil$, not $\lceil n\log_2 n\rceil$. For $n=5$: $5!=120$ leaves.
$2^6=64<120\le128=2^7$, so the height is at least 7.
$n\log_2 n$ is only the order of growth. The exact value is smaller because $\log_2 n!\approx n\log_2 n-1.44n+\tfrac12\log_2(2\pi n)$. For $n=5$ this gives $11.61-7.21+2.49\approx6.9$.
A cleverly ordered algorithm (merge insertion) really does sort 5 keys with 7 comparisons, so the bound is reached here.
examples.answer: 7 comparisons. The student answer of 12 uses the order of growth as if it were an exact value.

scenes.title: One pass of selection, bubble and insertion on [8,3,6,2,5]

steps.caption: Three copies of `[8, 3, 6, 2, 5]`. Each sort will do its own first pass.
**Selection:** scan all five keys (4 comparisons) and find the smallest, 2 at index 3. Swap it with index 0: `[2, 3, 6, 8, 5]`. One swap, and 2 is final.
**Bubble:** compare neighbours left to right. 8>3, 8>6, 8>2, 8>5 all swap, so 8 travels to the end: `[3, 6, 2, 5, 8]`. That is 4 comparisons and 4 swaps, and 8 is final.
**Insertion:** take the key 3 (index 1). The left key 8 is bigger, so shift 8 right and drop 3 into the gap: `[3, 8, 6, 2, 5]`. One comparison and one shift. Only the first two keys are sorted.
Selection fixes the **front**, bubble fixes the **back**, insertion fixes nothing yet but keeps a sorted prefix. The costs differ: 4 and 1 swap, 4 and 4, 1 and 1 shift.

scenes.title: Comparisons on reversed vs sorted input, n = 6

steps.caption: Reversed input: every pair is out of order. Selection makes 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15 comparisons, bubble makes 15, and insertion makes 15 because each key travels to the front.
Now the sorted input `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`. Selection does not look at the order of the data, so it still makes 15 comparisons.
Bubble with early exit: pass 1 compares 5 pairs, swaps nothing, and stops. That is 5 comparisons.
Insertion: each of the 5 later keys is compared once with its left neighbour and stays put. That is 5 comparisons.
Best case is $n-1=5$ for insertion and for bubble with early exit. The worst case is $\binom n2 = 15$ for all three. Selection has no best case.

The 6 remaining keys split 0 and 5, then 5 split 0 and 4. Those partitions cost 5 and 4. Running total: 6 + 5 + 4 = 15.
The chain goes on through 4, 3, 2 keys: 3 + 2 + 1 more. Total: 21 = $\binom 72$, with a recursion tree that is 7 levels deep.
Now a perfect median pivot on 7 keys. The split is 3 and 3, and the partition costs 6 comparisons. Running total: 6.
Each 3-key part splits 1 and 1 with 2 comparisons, so 2 + 2 = 4 more. Single keys cost nothing. Total: 6 + 4 = 10, with a tree that is only 3 levels deep.
Bad splits give $T(n)=T(n-1)+n-1=\Theta(n^2)$. Balanced splits give $T(n)=2T(n/2)+n-1=\Theta(n\log n)$. The recursion tree decides the cost.

scenes.title: Decision tree for sorting three keys

steps.caption: A comparison sort asks yes/no questions. The root asks "is $a<b$?". The left branch means yes and the right branch no.
Second level: if $a<b$ ask $b$ against $c$. If $a>b$ ask $a$ against $c$. Two leaves, `abc` and `bac`, can already be decided.
Third level: the remaining nodes ask one more question each and produce the leaves `acb`, `cab`, `bca` and `cba`.
Each leaf is one final order of the three keys. There are $3!=6$ possible orders, so the tree needs at least 6 leaves.
The longest root-to-leaf path has 3 comparisons. That is the worst case for this sort.
A binary tree of height $h$ has at most $2^h$ leaves. So $2^h\ge 6$ forces $h\ge\lceil\log_2 6\rceil=3$. No comparison sort for 3 keys can do better than 3 comparisons.
